items.title: George Lewis Interview, 1968-10-12
items.q: Chris Kelly. Straight. He just sort of was straight. He made a hard note. Chris Kelly was a... Couldn't make no hard notes.

ctx.x: So I went down to a four. Four is kind of hard. It's called a grain of the wood. Now here's a three and a half or three. But these have a more time. I found out this testing regime, you know what I mean? And then I found out that there's a lot of things that I found out. This testing regime, you know what I mean? It don't mean that the readers good. That's the only thing in there. I had to end this year, the slip, of course. But some diamond grain, you know. I was a king. Now for a card, I don't like. No classic…

the music better. You can hear the rhythm and the rhythm is the most important thing in the band. You can hear the rhythm. You got good rhythm. That's what Lawrence was living in. Fred could hear better. Joe. They did put on. You could hear the band and you only got the rhythm there. Joe said I worked him hard. I didn't work him hard. I mean he worked his own self hard. And then if you got the band you got the work man hard. Because most of the leaders don't want to work. They want to put their arm on their lap.…

I try to play in one way, the bands play in another. I like to play low register. I'm trying to play Mario Blasch. There was a mic that beat this one. Those old men didn't know mic in those days. But we played whenever we were. I had to play low register. There's one thing a text we're going to be running out soon. I wanted to mention, if you could say something about, and this is this time when you were playing out of Bunky, just before Bill Russell came down here in 42. Could you just say something about that…

items.title: George Lewis Interview, 1968-12-09
items.q: Well, I went up with Chris Kelly, uh, and, uh, they had a battle in Lafayette.

ctx.x: One thing I wanted to ask you about, which I did ask you about once before, but it was not, it was after the tape recorder gone out, is the time when, uh, the circumstances which led up to your playing with the E. Van Thomas Band. How did it come about that you went out there?

Oh, well, I did. Ruffin's, I remember mentioning that this, that this, poor man, poor man, not poor man, he's an ordinary poor, uh, Ruffins. I don't know what he meant with John, but every musician, you know, you would book dances. I was a musician, uh, Lafayette and Lafayette and Lafayette, and I'm up to Lafayette. Well, I went up with Chris Kelly, uh, and, uh, they had a battle in Lafayette. We had Thomas and Chris Kelly. Well, he vagued. I'll play Chris in the one set because he was a better musician than the…
But you had started a job when you, when he was killed. I mean, you had been paying for a job.

items.title: George Lewis Interview, 1968-11-25
items.q: I got, uh, Chris Kelly, Ramona. I played at, uh, Ramona.

ctx.x: So anyway, that was the first thing I wanted to ask you about, was about change of name, you know, Zeno, and when you changed it and why. Well, when I was born, my mother had several names, Francis, Joseph, Louis, Zeno. George was nowhere around. My mother had all the children that my mother had, two before me, they died. So my grandmother said, call this one George. My mother never had in her mind to call me George. But my grandma kept calling me George until my christening time when my mother went and had me…

I'll have to make it and play music, talk more with people and I find it's a good seat. So when Natalie was playing, he was playing, I was at the... I was playing my clarinet, same keys of trouble, but he didn't. Same keys of violin. Old shops and old flats. What about George like that? I would, a lot of him, I have a picture of him taking a job. Do you have a picture of yourself? Yeah, I remember Glenn, him, Bonk, me, him, Bonk, Marsman, Riley, Jim, and Dre, Elton, Mr. Tran, we played at the Academy of Music in…

items.title: George Lewis Interview, 1968-11-01
items.q: Well, every Tuesday, we've been at the booth.

ctx.x: He was a good trumpet player. Where did you mainly play with him? Where would these dancers be with him? How did I feel it? What I feel, what I feel, you know.
Well, every Tuesday, we've been at the booth. Yes, uh, I know you've been up there already.
It's called a L-stone. There's a white sort of, uh, plaster. Uh, somewhere off time, like Texas, Louisiana Avenue. And, uh, what was your Planket Dancers then? Hmm? Planket Dancers.
